meta.title: Who really said "Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Martin Luther King Jr. wrote it in his “Letter from Birmingham Jail,” April 16, 1963. Not from the “I Have a Dream” speech.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely MLK — from the 1963 “Letter from Birmingham Jail,” not the “I Have a Dream” speech. Verified against the letter’s text.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1929–1968 · Baptist minister & civil-rights leader, writing from jail in April 1963
answer.sourceLine: From King’s “Letter from Birmingham Jail,” dated April 16, 1963 — written in the margins of a newspaper while he was jailed for leading nonviolent protests. The line is confirmed in the widely published text of the letter, later collected in his 1964 book Why We Can’t Wait.

source.heading: Where the line comes from

docMeta.dd: May 1963 (American Friends Service Committee); collected in Why We Can’t Wait, 1964

source.excerpt: Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere. We are caught in an inescapable network of mutuality, tied in a single garment of destiny. Whatever affects one directly, affects all indirectly.
trail: The quote and its April 16, 1963 date are documented in Wikipedia’s article on the Letter from Birmingham Jail ↗, which also traces its 1963 publication history.
The fuller passage — “… an inescapable network of mutuality, tied in a single garment of destiny” — is reproduced from the letter on Goodreads ↗.
The Stanford King Institute ↗ hosts the annotated letter as part of the King Papers.
source.cutTag: ↑ the famous line is the opening of a longer sentence about “mutuality”
source.excerptNote: King wrote the line in response to being called an “outside agitator” — arguing that no community’s injustice can be treated as someone else’s problem.

author.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
author.heading: About Martin Luther King Jr.
author.bio: Martin Luther King Jr. (1929–1968) was a Baptist minister and the leading figure of the American civil-rights movement, an advocate of nonviolent resistance who led the Montgomery bus boycott and the 1963 March on Washington. He wrote the “Letter from Birmingham Jail” in April 1963 while jailed for civil-disobedience protests, and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964. He was assassinated in Memphis in 1968.

misattribution.heading: A real quote — but often mis-sourced
misattribution.intro: The attribution to King is correct. The common error is which of his works it comes from: the line is regularly assumed to be part of the August 1963 “I Have a Dream” address, or quoted with no source at all.

items.why: The line is not from the March on Washington address; it appears in the “Letter from Birmingham Jail,” written April 16, 1963 — more than four months before the August 28 speech, per Wikipedia ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: genuinely King’s words — from the Letter from Birmingham Jail ↗, April 16, 1963.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: King wrote the letter in response to a public statement by eight white Alabama clergymen who called his Birmingham campaign “unwise and untimely” and the work of an outsider. His answer — “Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere” — reframed the local protest as a matter of universal moral concern.
The sentence continues into one of King’s central ideas: that all people are “caught in an inescapable network of mutuality, tied in a single garment of destiny.”
